newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia guard vows toughness with Japan fishermen.
newsitem.headline: Russia guard vows toughness with Japan fishermen.

text.p: Russia's coast guard chief said on Tuesday his forces would continue to use force to keep Japanese poachers away from fish-rich waters around the disputed Southern Kurile Islands.

Admiral Innokenty Nalyotov, who is in charge of the naval branch of the Federal Borderguard Service, told a news briefing that his forces had managed to reduce the number of intrusions in Far East waters from 2,500 in 1992 to just 30 last year.
"We had only 10 violations of the border in the first half of 1997," he said. "We would have never had such progress if we did not treat intruders harshly."
Moscow has repeatedly accused Japanese fishing boats of poaching in its waters around the Russian-held Southern Kurile Islands, which Tokyo claims as its Northern Territories.
Last week Russian border guards opened fire on four Japanese boats that entered Russia's territorial waters near the islands, reportedly injuring several fishermen, one seriously.
Last August Russian patrol boats fired on two small Japanese fishing boats in the area, seriously injuring two crewmen.
Less serious incidents are fairly commonplace.
Japanese officials have complained that the Russian coastguards are over-reacting to intrusions of unarmed fishing vessels and have urged them not to use weapons to stop fishermen.
Nalyotov argues that his forces are acting in full accordance with international rules.

"The guards first send a radio warning to the intruder and order him to stop, then they repeat the orders with lights and flares, then they shoot in the air and only after all this does not work (do) they shoot to destroy the intruder," he said.
"Basically we want to create conditions so that potential violators would feel like dumping their plans before moving to carry them out."
But Moscow is keen not to allow last week's shooting incident to harm its steadily improving relations with Tokyo.

At a recent summit of the Group of Seven main industrialised nations in the U.S. city of Denver, President Boris Yeltsin told Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that Russia would no longer aim nuclear weapons at Japan.

On Tuesday Yeltsin held a telephone conversation with Japanese lawmaker Keizo Obuchi, an influential member of Hashimoto's ruling Liberal Democratic Party, and said it was time to step up bilateral contacts.
Obuchi was heading a delegation of Japanese businessmen and politicians to Moscow.
